docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The simulator is assumed to be perfect and there is no wind. The no-operation rollout and the rollout search both depend on the quality of the simulation, and search is usable in operations only if it runs faster than real time.
  • Only one aircraft type, the A320, is modelled.
  • The AMAN sequences were not produced by a real AMAN tool.
  • Fuel is not part of the reward.
  • Overflights and departures are not considered for separation.
  • Landing earlier than the AMAN target is penalised like landing late, which is not always desirable.

In operations the clearances would be suggestions to approach controllers through a human-machine interface. Such an interface was built for the multi-agent solution and tested with controllers in a real-time simulation, reported separately.

docs.title: Get the code
docs.text:
Summary

The public repository github.com/monadoy/tada holds both implementations, the trained models and the simulator. To run the single-agent code you need CPython 3.12 on Linux x86_64, the simulator wheel from artifacts/, and an A320 performance file that you must supply yourself because the data is licensed. This page lists what is in the repository and walks through the single-agent setup. The next two pages cover evaluation and training.

docs.title: What is in the repository
docs.text:
Path Contents single-agent/ The single-agent implementation described on this site: a JAX PPO learner with a windowed, autoregressive policy. Trained policies are saved as Stable-Baselines3 checkpoints and evaluated with PyTorch. multi_agent/ The multi-agent implementation: a shared policy trained with Ray RLlib and PyTorch. artifacts/single_agent/ The two published single-agent policies, mxp/ (TMB) and pms/ (PMS), each with its normalisation statistics and settings. artifacts/multi_agent/ The two published multi-agent policies, mxp/ and pms/. artifacts/simulator/wheels/ Flight simulator 0.2.80, built for CPython 3.12 on Linux, macOS (Apple Silicon) and Windows. Both implementations use it. docs/aircraft-designs.md The format of the aircraft performance file and where to put it.

Each implementation includes the scenario configuration and the seeds it needs. In file and directory names the repository uses the IATA codes of the two airports: mxp for Milan Malpensa (LIMC, trombone) and bgy for Milan Bergamo (LIME, point merge).

The software and models are research artefacts, shared as they are.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• CPython 3.12. The simulator wheels are built for this version only.
  • Linux x86_64 with glibc 2.34 or newer. The setup below is documented for Linux. Wheels for macOS and Windows are provided, but the simulator notes state that a wheel being available does not establish that the full training stack works on those systems. Use the Linux wheel inside WSL or a Linux container.
  • The simulator wheel for your platform, from artifacts/simulator/wheels/.
  • Aircraft performance data, which is not in the repository. See below.
  • A GPU is optional. Evaluation runs the policy with PyTorch on the CPU. Training runs its updates in JAX, on the CPU or on a CUDA device.

docs.title: 1. Clone and create an environment
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/monadoy/tada.git
cd tada/single-agent
python3.12 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate

Any Python 3.12 environment works. All commands on this page and the next two are run from single-agent/ unless stated otherwise.

docs.title: 2. Install the dependencies and the simulator
docs.text:
Copy the Linux wheel into simulator/wheels/ (create the directory, keep the filename) and install the CPU dependencies:

mkdir -p simulator/wheels
cp ../artifacts/simulator/wheels/flight_simulator-0.2.80-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_34_x86_64.whl simulator/wheels/
python -m pip install torch==2.8.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
sed 's/^jax\[cuda12\]/jax/' recipes/requirements-windowed.txt | python -m pip install -r /dev/stdin
python -m pip install simulator/wheels/flight_simulator-0.2.80-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_34_x86_64.whl

The sed substitution replaces the CUDA build of JAX with the CPU build. For training on a GPU, install the requirements file unchanged instead, with a compatible NVIDIA driver:

python -m pip install -r recipes/requirements-windowed.txt
python -m pip install simulator/wheels/flight_simulator-0.2.80-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_34_x86_64.whl

The requirements file pins jax 0.7.1, flax 0.12.0, optax 0.2.8, stable_baselines3 2.9.0 and gymnasium 1.1.1.

docs.title: 3. Supply the aircraft performance data
docs.text:
Aircraft performance data is licensed and is not distributed. Before running tests, training or evaluation, place it as A320.json in a designs/ directory under each scenario configuration:

for root in config/simulation_config_mxp config/simulation_config_bgy; do
  mkdir -p "$root/designs" && cp /path/to/A320.json "$root/designs/"
done

The simulator loads every *.json file in designs/ as one aircraft design, and the scenario generator uses the ICAO type A320. The file has this structure; every field is a required number unless shown as a string:

{
  "icao_typename": "A320",
  "descriptive_name": "AIRBUS A320-231",
  "masses": {"minimum_kg": 0.0, "reference_kg": 0.0, "maximum_kg": 0.0},
  "limits": {
    "max_longitudinal_acceleration_knots_per_sec": 0.0,
    "max_op_altitude_ft": 0.0,
    "v_stall_flap_kcas": 0.0,
    "v_stall_clean_kcas": 0.0,
    "v_mo_kcas": 0.0,
    "max_climb_rate_fpm": 0.0,
    "max_descent_rate_fpm": 0.0
  },
  "performance_sectors": [
    {
      "altitude_min_ft": 0.0,
      "altitude_max_ft": 2000.0,
      "cruise": {"v_opt_kcas": 0.0},
      "climb": {"v_opt_kcas": 0.0, "roc_fpm": 0.0},
      "descent": {"v_opt_kcas": 0.0, "rod_fpm": 0.0}
    }
  ]
}

performance_sectors lists altitude bands in ascending order. The published models were trained and evaluated with Airbus A320-231 values derived from EUROCONTROL BADA (Base of Aircraft Data), in five bands: 0 to 2000, 3000 to 8000, 10000 to 16000, 18000 to 24000 and 26000 to 33000 ft. That file has the SHA-256 checksum

466a0686dd1e181625fbef570c7dc0b433e0fdbc9f68188c0ffae0d63d850fcc

Other values change the simulated trajectories and therefore the results. The full description is in docs/aircraft-designs.md.

docs.title: 4. Verify the downloaded artefacts
docs.text:
From the repository root:

(cd artifacts/simulator && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS)
(cd artifacts/single_agent && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS)

docs.title: 5. Run the tests
docs.text:
pytest is not in the requirements file, so install it first:

python -m pip install pytest
TADA_SEQUENCE_OBS=1 TADA_MAX_PICKS=2 python -m pytest tests

The two variables select the configuration of the published models; they are explained under environment variables. tests/test_wheel_selection.py expects the Linux wheel in simulator/wheels/, as copied in step 2.

docs.title: Where things are in single-agent/
docs.text: Path Contents atc_env/, actions/, models/, network/ The environment, the clearance sets and masks, the observations and the policy network. jax_ppo/, main_jax.py The JAX learner and the training entry point. evaluation/ The rollout-search runner, the supplied evaluation seeds and the CSV export. analysis/ Policy-only scoring, the rollout search itself and episode recording. config/ Settings (config.py, windowed_config.py), the scenario configuration of each procedure and the training seed pool. simulator/, static/ Python adapters for the simulator and the sector definitions. tests/ Behaviour, compatibility, resume and numerical checks.

docs.title: The multi-agent code
docs.text: The multi-agent implementation has its own setup (it uses uv and a helper script), its own evaluation protocol and its own training configuration. They are documented in the multi-agent guide in the repository. The design is summarised on the multi-agent page, and the aircraft performance file is supplied in the same way, under multi_agent/config/simulation_config_mxp/designs/ and multi_agent/config/simulation_config_bgy/designs/. The multi-agent tools hash every file in the scenario configuration, so they accept only the exact file with the checksum given above, and designs/ must contain nothing else.

docs.title: Evaluate the published models
docs.text:
Summary

The paper evaluates each single-agent policy on 100 seeded scenarios of 20 arrivals, with 21 attempts per scenario, once with the policy alone and once with rollout search. Both runs can be repeated with the public code: python -m analysis.score_windowed scores the policy alone and python -m evaluation.run_search adds the search (8 candidates, replanning every 10 actions). An episode is solved when every flight lands within 60 s of its target and no loss of separation occurs. The supplied seeds were also used to select the published models, so the numbers are not an estimate on unseen scenarios.

Complete the setup first, including the aircraft performance file. All commands are run from single-agent/.

docs.title: The two models
docs.text:
The published policies are in artifacts/single_agent/.

Procedure Bundle TADA_ACTION_SET TADA_AIRPORT_MASK --procedure TMB, Milan Malpensa (LIMC) mxp/ v2 procedure tmb PMS, Milan Bergamo (LIME) pms/ v2pms empty pms

Each bundle holds three files that must stay together:

  • final_model.zip, the policy as a Stable-Baselines3 PPO checkpoint;
  • vecnormalize.pkl, the reward-normalisation statistics saved with it;
  • run_meta.json, the settings the policy was trained with. The evaluation tools read this file from the model's directory to build the same environment.

Both policies use the windowed environment with 20-flight streams, sequence observations, two picks per 45 s decision interval and the same reward settings. They differ in the clearance set and in the airport mask: the TMB policy was trained with the procedure mask, which blocks two of the 15 clearances (the smallest speed reduction and the larger speed increase), and the PMS policy without a mask.

Verify the files from the repository root:

(cd artifacts/single_agent && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS)

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Several settings size the observation and action spaces, so the code reads them from the environment when it is imported. They cannot be command-line flags. Set these once per shell:

export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES= TADA_GENERATOR=procedure
export TADA_SEQUENCE_OBS=1 TADA_MAX_PICKS=2 TADA_MASK_FRAME_FIX=1
Variable Value Meaning Default in the code TADA_ACTION_SET v2 or v2pms The clearance set: v2 for the trombone, v2pms for point merge. See Actions. v2 TADA_AIRPORT_MASK procedure or empty An optional mask that blocks some clearances of the set for one procedure. none TADA_SEQUENCE_OBS 1 Adds four AMAN-sequence features to each aircraft's observation. See Observations. 0 TADA_MAX_PICKS 2 Up to two clearances per decision interval (reselection). 1 TADA_MASK_FRAME_FIX 1 The coordinate frame used when clearance legality is computed. 1 TADA_GENERATOR procedure Scenarios are generated from the per-procedure configuration in config/simulation_config_mxp/ and config/simulation_config_bgy/. procedure CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES empty Hides any GPU. Evaluation runs on the CPU, one process per worker.

TADA_ACTION_SET and TADA_AIRPORT_MASK differ between the two models and are set on each command line below. Before an evaluation starts, the tools compare both with the model's run_meta.json and stop with a message naming the right value if they do not match. The sequence observations, the number of picks and the mask frame are then set from the checkpoint and its run_meta.json.

docs.title: The scenarios
docs.text:
evaluation/seeds.txt lists the 100 scenario seeds of the paper, one per line. A seed determines the whole scenario: the 20 arrivals, their routes and spawn times, and the AMAN sequence and target landing times. Random extra time-to-lose is disabled in the supplied generator configuration.

Pass the file with --seed-file evaluation/seeds.txt on every command. Without it the tools take the first seeds of config/eval_seeds.txt, which is a different list.

The evaluation seeds were used for model selection

Training does not draw these seeds: the supplied training pool contains none of them. They were, however, used to choose which trained policy to publish. Results on them are therefore optimistic compared with scenarios that played no part in development. Report success, safety and timing as separate metrics, as the repository's guides ask.

docs.title: Policy only
docs.text:
analysis/score_windowed.py flies each scenario with the policy alone and prints a summary.

mkdir -p runs/policy
TADA_ACTION_SET=v2 TADA_AIRPORT_MASK=procedure \
  python -m analysis.score_windowed \
  --models ../artifacts/single_agent/mxp/final_model.zip \
  --seed-file evaluation/seeds.txt --attempts 20 \
  --csv runs/policy/tmb_scores.csv
TADA_ACTION_SET=v2pms TADA_AIRPORT_MASK= \
  python -m analysis.score_windowed \
  --models ../artifacts/single_agent/pms/final_model.zip \
  --seed-file evaluation/seeds.txt --attempts 20 \
  --csv runs/policy/pms_scores.csv

Attempt 0 is the deterministic policy: at every decision it takes the most probable legal action. --attempts 20 adds 20 sampled attempts per seed, in which actions are drawn from the policy's distribution. All attempts of a seed fly the same scenario, and each sampled attempt has its own fixed random seed, so a run is repeatable. The procedure is read from run_meta.json; no procedure flag is needed.

The main options:

Option Default Meaning --models required One or more checkpoints. With several, the first is the reference and the others are compared with it seed by seed. They must share the same environment settings. --seed-file none File of scenario seeds, one per line. --seeds 100 Use only the first N seeds. --attempts 0 Sampled attempts per seed after the deterministic one. --flights 20 Arrivals per scenario. --workers CPU count minus 2 Parallel processes. --csv none Write one row per seed and attempt. The directory must exist. --flights-csv none Write one row per flight of the deterministic attempt, by position in the AMAN sequence.

python -m analysis.score_windowed --help lists the remaining options, which belong to development experiments (stitched streams, a critic-guided lookahead, a conflict shield) and are not part of the paper's protocol.

For each model the summary gives the number of solved seeds, the loss-of-separation rate with a 95% confidence interval, the share of flights on time, the clearances per episode and the mean landing deviation. With --attempts it also gives the share of seeds solved by at least one attempt.

To record the per-aircraft data that the CSV export needs, run the same episodes through analysis/evaluation_records.py:

TADA_ACTION_SET=v2 TADA_AIRPORT_MASK=procedure \
  python -m analysis.evaluation_records \
  --model ../artifacts/single_agent/mxp/final_model.zip \
  --seed-file evaluation/seeds.txt --attempts 20 \
  --out-prefix runs/policy/policy_tmb

Use v2pms, an empty mask, the pms/ model and --out-prefix runs/policy/policy_pms for point merge. Its --attempts defaults to 10, so state 20 explicitly.

docs.title: Policy with rollout search
docs.text:
Rollout search uses the simulator to look ahead. At each planning point it rolls several candidate continuations to the end of the episode on copies of the simulation, keeps the best, executes its first actions and plans again.

Rollout search with K = 8 candidates and M = 10. The first 10 actions of the best candidate are executed; the rest of it becomes the incumbent plan at the next planning point. 
TADA_ACTION_SET=v2 TADA_AIRPORT_MASK=procedure \
  python -m evaluation.run_search --procedure tmb \
  --model ../artifacts/single_agent/mxp/final_model.zip \
  --seed-file evaluation/seeds.txt --out runs/search
TADA_ACTION_SET=v2pms TADA_AIRPORT_MASK= \
  python -m evaluation.run_search --procedure pms \
  --model ../artifacts/single_agent/pms/final_model.zip \
  --seed-file evaluation/seeds.txt --out runs/search

Output file names start with the procedure, so both runs can share one directory. That is what the CSV export expects.

Option Default Meaning --model required The checkpoint. --procedure required tmb or pms. --seed-file none File of scenario seeds. --seeds 100 Use only the first N seeds. --attempts 0-20 Attempt indices: a range such as 0-20 or 1-5, or a single index such as 0. --K 8 Candidates per planning point, including the incumbent plan. --M 10 Policy actions executed between planning points. A second pick within a decision interval counts as an action, so 10 actions can span fewer than 10 intervals. --flights 20 Arrivals per scenario. --workers 12 Parallel processes. --out runs/search Output directory. --picks off Also write one row per executed action. --resume off Continue an interrupted run.

The defaults give 100 seeds times 21 attempts, 2100 episodes per procedure. Episodes are flown attempt by attempt, so a partial run already covers every seed at attempt 0.

How the search behaves, as implemented in analysis/rollout_search.py:

  • At the first planning point the incumbent plan is the deterministic policy's rollout and the other seven candidates are sampled. At later points the candidates are the incumbent, one deterministic rollout and six sampled rollouts.
  • Candidates are ranked by their outcome at the end of the episode, in this order: no loss of separation, more flights within 60 s, smaller total absolute deviation, fewer clearances. A new candidate replaces the incumbent only if it is strictly better.
  • No further candidates are generated at a planning point once the best one solves the episode. A rollout is abandoned as soon as it can no longer match the best candidate's number of on-time flights; this pruning does not change which candidate is chosen.
  • The attempt index only changes the random seeds of the sampled candidates. Attempt 0 uses the base seeding; attempts 1 to 20 repeat the search on the same scenario with different samples. Every attempt starts from the deterministic rollout, so with search an attempt is never a purely sampled episode.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
run_search writes these files to the output directory, where <proc> is tmb or pms:

File Rows Main columns <proc>_episodes.csv One per seed and attempt solved, sep (loss of separation), on_time (share of flights within 60 s), all_on_time, hard_solved (as solved, within 30 s), landed, n_flights, mean_dev, max_dev, end_reason, clearances, warning_pairs, the search cost (n_plans, n_rollouts, rollout_steps, wall_s) and one count per clearance (n_SLOW_DOWN_SMALL, ...). <proc>_aircraft.csv One per flight aircraft_index (position in the AMAN sequence, 0 to 19), aman_ttl_s (TTL positive, TTG negative), initial_dev_s, final_dev_s, final_source, clearances. <proc>_picks.csv One per executed action, with --picks t_s, pick_in_interval (1 or 2), callsign, clearance, kind. <proc>_run_settings.json The seeds, attempts, K, M and environment settings of the run, with SHA-256 checksums of the model, its metadata, the scenario configuration, the sector files and the simulator library.

Deviations are in seconds, landing time minus target, so a positive value is late. initial_dev_s is the deviation forecast at the start of the episode if no clearance is ever issued. final_dev_s is the realised deviation when final_source is landed; if the episode ended before the flight landed it is a forecast (predicted) or unknown (unresolved). warning_pairs counts the aircraft pairs with an infringement that did not become a loss of separation. end_reason is one of success, delayed, timeout, airspace_exit and separation.

evaluation_records writes <prefix>_extra.csv and <prefix>_extra_aircraft.csv with the same information for the policy alone, and two summary sheets, <prefix>_per_episode.csv and <prefix>_per_aircraft.csv.

docs.title: Resuming
docs.text:
An interrupted search run can be continued. Start it again with exactly the same command plus --resume:

TADA_ACTION_SET=v2 TADA_AIRPORT_MASK=procedure \
  python -m evaluation.run_search --procedure tmb \
  --model ../artifacts/single_agent/mxp/final_model.zip \
  --seed-file evaluation/seeds.txt --out runs/search --resume

The run continues only if its settings are identical to those in <proc>_run_settings.json, checksums included. Seed and attempt pairs whose episode and aircraft rows are complete are skipped; rows of an episode that was cut off are removed and the episode is flown again. Without --resume the tool refuses to write into a directory that already holds results for that procedure.

docs.title: CSV export
docs.text:
evaluation/export_csv.py converts the raw files into two sheets, one row per episode and one row per aircraft. The first column of each sheet is the agent type, so single- and multi-agent results can be combined in one table.

python -m evaluation.export_csv --agent search --raw runs --out runs/sheets
python -m evaluation.export_csv --agent policy --raw runs/policy --out runs/sheets
--agent Reads from --raw search search/<proc>_episodes.csv and search/<proc>_aircraft.csv best (default) <proc>_episodes.csv and <proc>_aircraft.csv directly in --raw policy policy_<proc>_extra.csv and policy_<proc>_extra_aircraft.csv

--seed-file sets the row order and defaults to evaluation/seeds.txt; --attempts keeps attempts 0 to N and defaults to 20. For each agent the tool writes TADA_single_agent_<agent> - Per Episode.csv and TADA_single_agent_<agent> - Per Aircraft.csv, and a copy of each without the header row. The per-episode sheet has the end reason, the total initial and final absolute deviation, whether the AMAN sequence was met, whether an infringement without loss of separation occurred, and the number of clearances by type. The per-aircraft sheet has the TTL or TTG, the initial and final absolute deviation, whether the flight landed in its AMAN position and its number of clearances.

An episode whose aircraft rows are incomplete is skipped with a count in the output. Check that every expected seed and attempt is present before using the sheets.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
The paper reports three outcomes per episode. They are computed by the environment from the live simulation, not from forecasts.

Metric Definition Column Solved Every flight landed within 60 s of its AMAN target landing time, and no loss of separation occurred. solved Loss of separation Two aircraft came closer than 3 NM horizontally and 500 ft vertically at the same time. The episode ends there, and flights still airborne count as not on time. sep On time The share of all flights in the scenario that landed within 60 s of their target. on_time

Counting, for each seed, whether any of its attempts solved it gives the share of episodes solved with at least one attempt, which the paper plots against the number of attempts. The figures themselves are on the Results page.

When single- and multi-agent results are compared, the search budgets differ and should be stated: the multi-agent guide evaluates its search with K = 8 and M = 1.

docs.title: Train a policy
docs.text:
Summary

single-agent/main_jax.py trains a policy with PPO and writes Stable-Baselines3 checkpoints that the evaluation tools load directly. The procedure is chosen by the action set and the use case; the reward, the traffic curriculum, the seeds and the optimiser are command-line options. The paper's curriculum of 10 flights for the first 2.5 million transitions and 20 afterwards is one --curriculum argument. A run is stored under experiments/ with its settings, so a trained model can be scored without further configuration.

Complete the setup first. For training on a GPU, install the unchanged requirements file as described there. All commands are run from single-agent/.

docs.title: A first run
docs.text:
Training uses the same environment variables as evaluation:

export TADA_GENERATOR=procedure
export TADA_SEQUENCE_OBS=1 TADA_MAX_PICKS=2 TADA_MASK_FRAME_FIX=1

Choose the device before starting Python: export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES= (empty) trains on the CPU, and leaving the variable unset or naming a device lets JAX use the GPU.

The repository's guide gives a short example for the trombone at Milan Malpensa:

TADA_ACTION_SET=v2 TADA_AIRPORT_MASK=procedure \
  python main_jax.py --env windowed --reward-mode outcome_pbrs \
  --use-case 1 --flights 20 --seed 42 \
  --train-seed-pool config/training_seeds/training_seeds.txt \
  --n-envs 4 --total-timesteps 1000000 --run-suffix mxp

and the same for point merge at Milan Bergamo, with the other action set, no airport mask and use case 2:

TADA_ACTION_SET=v2pms TADA_AIRPORT_MASK= \
  python main_jax.py --env windowed --reward-mode outcome_pbrs \
  --use-case 2 --flights 20 --seed 42 \
  --train-seed-pool config/training_seeds/training_seeds.txt \
  --n-envs 4 --total-timesteps 1000000 --run-suffix pms

With four workers and one million transitions this is a quick example that the pipeline works, not the paper's training budget. It also uses the default reward settings, which differ from those of the published models; see below.

docs.title: What a run does
docs.text:
--n-envs worker processes each run one windowed environment. Together they collect a rollout of 4096 transitions, so --n-envs must divide 4096. The learner then updates the policy on that rollout, and the cycle repeats until --total-timesteps transitions have been collected.

These PPO settings are fixed in main_jax.py and are the ones listed in the paper:

Setting Value Rollout buffer 4096 transitions, shared by all workers Minibatch size 256 Optimisation epochs 5 Clip range 0.2 Discount γ 0.998 (1 for a zero-time reselection transition) GAE λ 0.95 Maximum gradient norm 1.5 Normalisation rewards yes, observations no

The learning rate rises linearly from zero to --lr-max over the first --warmup-frac of training and then follows a half cosine down to --final-lr.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
python main_jax.py --help prints the full list. The options below are grouped by purpose; where no default is shown, the option is off or unset.

Procedure and traffic

Option Default Meaning --env windowed windowed is the published design. default is an earlier environment without the temporal window. --use-case 1 1 is the trombone at Milan Malpensa, 2 is point merge at Milan Bergamo. Combine it with the matching TADA_ACTION_SET. --flights 20 Arrivals per scenario. --curriculum Traffic stages within one run; see the curriculum. --seed 0 Seeds the initial weights and the training scenarios; see seeds. --train-seed-pool Draw training scenarios from a file of seeds instead of at random. --train-max-early-s Redraw a training scenario while the do-nothing forecast has a flight landing more than this many seconds early. --stitch-segments, --stitch-gap 1 segment; gap 120 to 900 s Join several generated scenarios into one longer stream, separated by a random gap. Not used for the published models.

Reward and environment

Option Default Meaning --reward-mode legacy outcome_pbrs is the reward of the paper: landing brackets, a cost per clearance, a terminal penalty and potential-based shaping (Objective). It is required when TADA_MAX_PICKS is above 1. --hard-bracket Adds the top landing bracket: 4 for a landing within 30 s. The terminal penalty rises from 90 to 100 with it. --release-locked Releases flights from the front of the window once they are locked: under control, forecast to land within --release-dev-s of the target, and in no forecast conflict. --release-dev-s 30 The threshold for --release-locked, in seconds. --pay-at-release Pays a flight's bracket value when it is released, from its forecast deviation, and corrects it at touchdown. Needs --release-locked. --flat-deviation The deviation potential counts every flight whose landing the forecast resolves at full weight. --pbrs-flat The sequence and conflict potentials without their time ramps. --violation-penalty Overrides the terminal penalty.

Optimiser

Option Default Meaning --total-timesteps 5,000,000 Transitions to collect. --n-envs 16 Worker processes. Must divide 4096. --lr-max, --final-lr 3e-4, 3e-5 Peak and final learning rate. --warmup-frac 0.08 Share of training used for the linear warm-up. --ent-coef 0.01 Entropy coefficient. --vf-coef 0.25 Value-loss coefficient. --target-kl 0.05 Updates on a rollout stop early when the approximate KL divergence reaches this value.

Run management

Option Default Meaning --run-suffix Text appended to the run directory's name. --save-freq 25,000 Transitions between checkpoints. --init-weights, --critic-warmup-steps, --critic-warmup-lr Warm starts.

docs.title: The settings of the published models
docs.text:
Each published bundle records its environment settings in run_meta.json. They correspond to these options, for both procedures:

--env windowed --reward-mode outcome_pbrs --flights 20
--hard-bracket --release-locked --release-dev-s 30 --pay-at-release --flat-deviation

with TADA_SEQUENCE_OBS=1, TADA_MAX_PICKS=2 and TADA_MASK_FRAME_FIX=1; action set v2 with the procedure airport mask for the trombone, and v2pms with no mask and --use-case 2 for point merge. The reward given in the paper, with its top bracket at 30 s and its penalty of 100, is the one selected by --hard-bracket.

docs.title: The curriculum
docs.text:
The paper trains for ten million transitions with 32 parallel environments: 10 flights per scenario for the first 2.5 million transitions, then 20. The short streams make credit assignment easier while the policy learns what the clearances do; the longer ones make it learn how flights replace one another in the window.

--curriculum expresses this directly. Its value is a comma-separated list of stages, each written flights:segments:until_step, where segments is the number of stitched scenarios (1 for a single scenario) and until_step is the transition count at which the stage ends:

TADA_ACTION_SET=v2 TADA_AIRPORT_MASK=procedure \
  python main_jax.py --env windowed --reward-mode outcome_pbrs \
  --hard-bracket --release-locked --pay-at-release --flat-deviation \
  --use-case 1 --seed 42 \
  --curriculum "10:1:2500000,20:1:10000000" \
  --train-seed-pool config/training_seeds/training_seeds.txt \
  --n-envs 32 --total-timesteps 10000000 --run-suffix mxp

For point merge, change the action set, the mask and the use case as in the first example.

This command combines the schedule described in the paper with the settings recorded in the bundles. The bundles do not record the seed, the seed pool or the schedule of the runs that produced them, so it is the documented recipe, not a guarantee of reproducing the published weights.

How the stages work:

  • The stage boundaries must increase, and the last must reach --total-timesteps.
  • At a boundary only the environment workers are replaced. The policy, the optimiser state, the reward-normalisation statistics and the learning-rate schedule carry over.
  • The stage values replace --flights and --stitch-segments.
  • A stage may name its own seed file as a fourth field, flights:segments:until_step:pool, which replaces --train-seed-pool for that stage. This allows a curriculum over scenario difficulty as well as length.
  • --curriculum needs --env windowed and fewer than 100 workers.

docs.title: Seeds and seed pools
docs.text:
--seed fixes two things: the initial network weights, and the scenarios each worker sees. Worker i draws its scenario seeds from its own generator, seeded with seed × 1000 + i (plus 100 × stage under a curriculum). The sequence of training scenarios is therefore determined by --seed, --n-envs and the curriculum.

Where the scenario seeds come from depends on --train-seed-pool:

  • With a pool, each new episode takes a seed drawn at random from the file. The repository supplies config/training_seeds/training_seeds.txt, a pool of 40,000 seeds, one per line. It is used for both procedures.
  • Without a pool, each new episode takes a random 31-bit seed.

In both cases the seeds listed in config/eval_seeds.txt are never used for training, and the supplied pool contains none of the seeds in evaluation/seeds.txt.

--train-max-early-s is an alternative to a pool: it filters scenarios during training by generating each one and redrawing it if a flight is forecast to land too early. A pool of seeds screened in advance avoids that work in the training loop.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
A run is named atc_run_1_<N>, with the next free number and the --run-suffix if one is given. Everything it writes is under experiments/:

experiments/atc_run_1_<N>_<suffix>/
├── run_meta.json                                  settings of the run
├── checkpoints/
│   ├── ppo_tada_<steps>_steps.zip                 policy, every --save-freq transitions
│   └── ppo_tada_vecnormalize_<steps>_steps.pkl    its reward-normalisation statistics
├── tb/                                            TensorBoard events and progress.csv
├── final_model.zip                                policy at the end of training
└── vecnormalize.pkl

The TensorBoard logs are in the run's own tb/ directory. A top-level tb_logs/ directory, if one exists, is only consulted when the next run number is chosen. The trainer also creates two directories it does not write to, best/ and eval_logs/.

run_meta.json records the action set, the airport mask, the observation and reselection settings, the reward and environment options, the seed, the curriculum and the optimiser settings. The evaluation tools look for it next to a model or one directory above, so both final_model.zip and the files in checkpoints/ can be scored as they are:

TADA_ACTION_SET=v2 TADA_AIRPORT_MASK=procedure \
  python -m analysis.score_windowed \
  --models experiments/atc_run_1_<N>_mxp/final_model.zip \
  --seed-file evaluation/seeds.txt

To follow a run:

tensorboard --logdir experiments/atc_run_1_<N>_mxp/tb

Useful series are custom_metrics/success_rolling and window_metrics/on_time_rate for the outcome of training episodes, window_metrics/clearances for the number of clearances, rollout/ep_rew_mean for the return, train/approx_kl and train/learning_rate for the optimiser, and time/fps for throughput. Under a curriculum, time/curriculum_stage shows the current stage. Training episodes are sampled from the policy on training scenarios, so these series are not the evaluation scores of a checkpoint; score a checkpoint as shown above.

Stopping a run with Ctrl-C saves latest_model.zip and latest_vecnormalize.pkl in the run directory. There is no option to resume a run with its optimiser state; a new run can start from saved weights as described next.

docs.title: Warm starts
docs.text:
--init-weights starts a run from the weights of an existing checkpoint instead of random weights. The checkpoint's network may be narrower than the new one in two supported ways: it may lack the sequence observations or the reselection input, in which case the new input columns start at zero, and it may lack the reselection head, which then starts with a small probability of asking for a second pick. The new policy therefore begins close to the behaviour of the old one. Any other difference in shape is an error.

When the reward differs from the one the checkpoint was trained on, its value estimates are on the wrong scale and the first updates can erase the policy. Two options guard against this, as the paper describes:

  • --critic-warmup-steps N trains only the value head for the first N transitions, at the constant learning rate --critic-warmup-lr (default 3e-4). The rest of the network is then unfrozen with a fresh optimiser state, and the normal schedule runs over the remaining transitions.
  • A peak learning rate ten times lower than for training from scratch.

The example in main_jax.py combines them:

python main_jax.py --env windowed --reward-mode outcome_pbrs \
  --init-weights experiments/<run>/checkpoints/ppo_tada_<N>_steps.zip \
  --n-envs 16 --critic-warmup-steps 100000 --lr-max 3e-5 --final-lr 3e-6 \
  --ent-coef 0.003 --total-timesteps 5000000 --run-suffix windowed_jax

A warm start copies weights only. The reward-normalisation statistics and the optimiser state of the earlier run are not loaded.

The published reference recipe trains from random weights. How warm starts were used during development is described in the Research notes.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
The public files do not state a required machine or an expected training time; the repository's guide says to choose the worker count and the training budget for your hardware. What they do state:

  • Each of the --n-envs workers is a separate process running the simulator on the CPU.
  • The PPO updates run in JAX. With the CUDA build of JAX they run on the GPU; with the CPU build the same code runs without one.
  • main_jax.py sets XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false unless you set it yourself, so JAX allocates GPU memory as needed instead of reserving it all.
  • Evaluation always runs the policy with PyTorch on the CPU.

The paper's runs used 32 parallel environments. Timings measured during development are in the Research notes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Summary

Both approaches use the same framework: a deterministic flight simulator wrapped in an environment that encodes observations, masks infeasible clearances, evaluates the reward and ends the episode. A decision is taken every 45 s. Policies are actor-critic networks trained with PPO, one per procedure. The approaches differ in their view of the airspace: the single agent sees a window of ten flights and chooses both the aircraft and its clearance; in the multi-agent approach every aircraft is an agent of one shared policy and a rule chooses which aircraft act.

The framework shared by both approaches. The predicted world is a copy of the live world that is rolled forward without new clearances after every transition.

docs.title: One framework, two views of the airspace
docs.text:
Single-agent Multi-agent Agent one, for the whole airspace one per aircraft, sharing one policy Observation a window of the next 10 flights in the AMAN sequence, in one aircraft tensor, with action history ego-centric: one aircraft, its route and its five most relevant neighbours Who acts the policy picks the aircraft, then its clearance a rule picks the aircraft; the policy picks the clearance Clearances per 45 s up to 2 (reselection) up to 3, one per sector group Policy network larger, sees more flights; simpler credit assignment compact, recurrent; generalises across callsigns, routes and traffic density Implementation JAX PPO, policies loadable with Stable-Baselines3 Ray RLlib and PyTorch

Separate policies are trained for Milan Malpensa (LIMC, trombone, TMB) and Milan Bergamo (LIME, point merge, PMS). Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) with an actor-critic network was chosen for its stable updates, its robustness in high-dimensional state spaces and its fit with discrete action spaces.

docs.title: Live world and predicted world
docs.text: The simulator runs at two levels. The live world flies the spawned aircraft and applies clearances. The predicted world is a copy of it that is rolled forward with no further clearances (the no-operation rollout, or do-nothing forecast). It tells the environment what would happen if the agent stopped acting now: each flight's predicted landing time and deviation, and every predicted infringement with its severity and its time. Observations and rewards are built from that forecast, so the agent is shown, and paid for, the consequences of its clearances rather than the current positions alone.

docs.title: Decisions and clearances
docs.text:
The environment is acted on once every 45 s, which reflects how often a controller can issue clearances. A decision selects one or more aircraft and then a clearance for each. Choosing the clearance given the aircraft matters because the feasible clearances differ a great deal between two aircraft in the same situation, and it avoids spending probability on aircraft-clearance combinations that cannot be executed.

On the trombone the clearance types are:

  • Do nothing. No command; the aircraft keeps its speed and route.
  • Change speed. Indicated airspeed up or down in multiples of 10 kt: the main control for timing and gentle spacing.
  • Turn and rejoin. Steer 40° off course, fly a fixed distance, then rejoin the route further downstream. It delays the aircraft and creates lateral spacing.
  • Extend or retract the trombone. Lengthen or shorten the downwind leg by one segment.
  • Skip waypoints. Cut one or more upcoming waypoints, where that is a shortcut within the planned route.
  • Vector to ILS. Intercept the ILS and join the final approach.

On the point merge, extend or retract trombone becomes extend or retract the PMS arc (multi-agent only) and vector to ILS becomes direct to merge point: the aircraft leaves the sequencing leg and flies straight to the merge point.

Route-related clearances on (a) the trombone and (b) the point merge.

The exact single-agent action sets are on Actions and reselection; the multi-agent set is on Multi-agent approach.

docs.title: Action masking
docs.text: At every decision the environment computes which clearances are legal for each aircraft, from aircraft limits, waypoint constraints, route geometry and waypoint availability. Masking is not an oracle: it removes commands that are physically or procedurally invalid, not commands that turn out badly. For example, a speed change is offered only if it respects the speed restrictions, a waypoint can be skipped only if the route still has it, and in the multi-agent solution an aircraft on the PMS arc cannot be vectored. Illegal actions are given a vanishing probability, so they are never sampled and PPO never learns from probability mass placed on choices the environment would have rejected.

docs.title: Reward priorities
docs.text:
Both approaches use a dense, shaped reward with the same order of priorities:

  1. Safety. The dominant term penalises predicted infringements, weighted by their geometry and by how soon they are predicted, and a realised loss of separation ends the episode.
  2. Landing precision. Reducing the predicted absolute time deviation is rewarded, per aircraft and over the whole set.
  3. Action efficiency. Every active clearance costs a small penalty. In the multi-agent solution the cost depends on the type of clearance.

The single-agent reward is on Objective and reward.

docs.title: Episodes
docs.text: An episode ends when all aircraft have landed, when a conflict occurs, when an aircraft leaves the airspace, or when the step limit is reached. Details for the single agent are on Episodes and windowing.

docs.title: At inference: policy alone or with rollout search
docs.text: A trained policy can be used on its own, deterministically or by sampling, or as the proposal distribution of a rollout search: a policy-guided form of model predictive control that compares several full continuations of the episode in the simulator and executes the start of the best one.

docs.title: Actions and reselection
docs.text:
Summary

A decision is a pair, (aircraft, clearance), drawn from a discrete set of 15 clearances. There are two sets, one per procedure: v2 for the trombone and v2pms for point merge. They differ in the clearances that work on the delay-absorption structure. Masks remove every choice that cannot be flown before the policy samples. The policy picks the aircraft first, then a clearance for that aircraft, then decides whether to pick again. With reselection it can clear a second aircraft inside the same 45 s interval, after seeing the forecast effect of the first clearance.

Source: single-agent/actions/ (actions_v2.py, actions_v2pms.py, action_mask_v2.py, action_mask_v2pms.py, action_set.py), single-agent/network/autoregressive_policy.py, single-agent/atc_env/windowed_env.py.

docs.title: What a decision is
docs.text:
The action is a triple of integers, (aircraft, clearance, again):

  • aircraft: one of the 10 window slots;
  • clearance: one of 15 clearances, to be applied to the aircraft in that slot;
  • again: 1 to request another pick before simulated time advances, 0 to execute now.

The action space is MultiDiscrete([10, 15, 2]). The third component exists when reselection is enabled (TADA_MAX_PICKS=2), as it is for both published policies.

docs.title: The two clearance sets
docs.text:
Clearances depend on the procedure, so each published policy has its own set. Both sets have 15 entries and share the slot numbers, which keeps the network the same size for both procedures.

Route-related clearances on (a) the trombone and (b) the point merge system. The single-agent point merge set does not lengthen or shorten the arc: its flights start on the full arc and leave it with a direct to the merge point. # clearance effect TMB (v2) PMS (v2pms) 0 DO_NOTHING no command; the aircraft keeps its speed and route yes yes 1 SLOW_DOWN_SMALL target speed −10 kt blocked by the airport mask yes 2 SLOW_DOWN_MEDIUM target speed −20 kt yes yes 3 SLOW_DOWN_LARGE target speed −30 kt yes yes 4 SPEED_UP_SMALL target speed +10 kt yes yes 5 SPEED_UP_MEDIUM target speed +20 kt blocked by the airport mask yes 6 TURN_LEFT_AND_RETURN_TO_ROUTE 40° left for 10 NM, then rejoin yes yes 7 TURN_RIGHT_AND_RETURN_TO_ROUTE 40° right for 10 NM, then rejoin yes yes 8 LENGTHEN_TROMBONE add one trombone level yes never legal 9 SHORTEN_TROMBONE remove one added trombone level yes never legal 10 SKIP_1_WAYPOINT drop the next waypoint yes yes 11 SKIP_2_WAYPOINTS_NOT_NEXT keep the next waypoint, drop the 2 after it yes yes 12 SKIP_3_WAYPOINTS_NOT_NEXT keep the next waypoint, drop the 3 after it yes yes 13 SKIP_4_WAYPOINTS_NOT_NEXT keep the next waypoint, drop the 4 after it yes yes 14 VECTOR_TO_ILS (TMB) / DIRECT_TO_MERGE_POINT (PMS) leave the structure for the final approach vector to ILS direct to merge point

"Yes" means the clearance belongs to the set that the published policy uses. Whether it is legal for a given aircraft at a given moment is decided by the masks.

The two sets differ in three slots:

  • Slot 14 is VECTOR_TO_ILS on the trombone and DIRECT_TO_MERGE_POINT on point merge.
  • Slots 8 and 9 lengthen and shorten the trombone. They have no meaning on point merge and are never legal there. They keep their slots and names so that both sets have the same width.
  • The starting route differs. A trombone flight starts on the short AMAN route and is delayed by lengthening the trombone. A point merge flight starts with its whole sequencing leg and is taken off it by the direct-to (The problem).

The speed, turn and skip clearances are the same code in both sets.

The set is chosen by the environment variable TADA_ACTION_SET (v2 or v2pms, default v2), which is read when the code is imported. A model records its set in run_meta.json, and loading it under the other set stops with an error that names the variable to change. The design history of the set, including an earlier one with 22 clearances, is in the Research notes.

docs.title: What each clearance does
docs.text:
Do nothing. No command is issued. The aircraft keeps its current speed and route. It is free: only real clearances carry the action cost.

Change speed. The clearance moves the aircraft's target speed by −10, −20, −30, +10 or +20 kt. There are three steps down and two up. A slow-down is legal when the new target stays at or above the aircraft's minimum speed. A speed-up is legal when the new target stays at or below its maximum speed and does not exceed the target speed of the next waypoint.

Turn and rejoin. The aircraft leaves its route on a heading 40° to the left or right of its target heading, flies that heading for the time it takes to cover 10 NM, and then resumes the route towards the same next waypoint. The clearance delays the aircraft and moves it sideways, which makes it the tool for opening lateral spacing. A turn is legal when the leg is flyable: from the end of the 10 NM leg, the turn back to the next waypoint is at most 90°, and the track change at that waypoint is at most 95°. The direction convention of this test is selected by TADA_TURN_MASK_FIX; a model's run_meta.json decides the setting when the model is loaded, and the published policies use the default. The rejoin is a command scheduled for later, so a decision step that issues a turn lasts until the rejoin plus the usual 45 s.

Lengthen or shorten the trombone (TMB). Lengthen adds one level to the downwind leg: one waypoint outbound and its partner inbound. It can be repeated up to the trombone's four levels and is legal while the aircraft has not passed the point where the next level begins. Shorten removes the most recently added level and is legal while that level is still entirely ahead of the aircraft. The two are exact inverses. Shortening cannot go below the short AMAN route.

Skip waypoints. SKIP_1_WAYPOINT drops the next waypoint, so the aircraft flies direct to the one after it. The other three keep the next waypoint and drop the 2, 3 or 4 that follow it. A skip is legal when at least four waypoints remain beyond the point where the route is rejoined and the track change there is at most 95°. A skip shortens the route when the dropped waypoints formed a detour.

Vector to ILS (TMB). The aircraft's route is replaced by its last four waypoints, which takes it off the downwind leg and onto the final approach. It is legal once the aircraft is on the trombone and has not yet started the leg back towards the airport, subject to the same 95° limit.

Direct to merge point (PMS). The aircraft leaves the sequencing arc and flies to the merge point, then continues on the rest of its route. It is legal while the aircraft is on its sequencing leg: it has passed the arc point where its leg begins, and only arc points lie between it and the merge point.

Every route clearance (turn, skip, lengthen, shorten, vector to ILS, direct to merge point) also requires more than four waypoints left in the route.

docs.title: The procedure airport mask
docs.text:
An optional mask can block clearances for a whole procedure. It is selected with TADA_AIRPORT_MASK and defined in AIRPORT_MASKS in single-agent/actions/action_set.py. The one mask defined there is called procedure.

For the trombone set it blocks two clearances at Malpensa:

  • SLOW_DOWN_SMALL (−10 kt);
  • SPEED_UP_MEDIUM (+20 kt).

The published TMB policy was trained and is evaluated with this mask, so its speed clearances are −20 kt, −30 kt and +10 kt. The mask is combined with the legality mask below by a logical AND. If that leaves an aircraft with no legal clearance, DO_NOTHING is made legal again.

The published PMS policy uses no airport mask (AIRPORT_MASKS also has a row for v2pms, which that policy does not use). A model's mask is recorded in its run_meta.json together with the clearance set, and loading the model under a different mask stops with an error.

docs.title: Masking
docs.text:
Masks decide what can be sampled. They serve two purposes: they keep commands that cannot be flown out of the simulator, and they keep the learning algorithm from spending probability on choices that the environment would reject or ignore. The masks are not an oracle. They test whether a clearance can be executed, not whether it is a good idea.

The observation carries three masks:

mask shape allows mask_action_per_ac 10 × 15 the clearances that are legal for each slot mask_select 10 the slots that may be picked at this pick mask_again 1 whether another pick may be requested

Clearance mask. A row starts from the rules in the previous section: aircraft speed limits, waypoint constraints, route geometry and what is left of the delay-absorption structure. Four further rules apply:

  • A flight that the forecast puts in a conflict within the next 2880 s cannot be left alone: DO_NOTHING is removed from its row.
  • A pending flight, which has not entered the terminal area, can only be given DO_NOTHING.
  • A released flight that is shown at the tail of a stream can only be given DO_NOTHING.
  • A flight that was already cleared in this decision interval can only be given DO_NOTHING until the clock moves.

Selection mask. Only flights under control that have not yet been cleared in this decision interval can be picked. If no flight in the window is under control, any occupied slot can be picked, and its only legal clearance is DO_NOTHING.

Again mask. Another pick can be requested only if the pick budget is not used up (two picks per interval) and another aircraft would still be available to clear.

The policy reads the masks from the observation and applies them to its logits before sampling, and again when the learner evaluates the stored actions. A masked choice is never sampled.

docs.title: Sampling an action
docs.text:
An action is sampled in three stages. Each stage is conditioned on the stages before it, and each is masked to what is legal at that point.

1 · which aircraft slots 1 … 10 (AMAN order) hollow = masked: pending / cleared a 2 · which clearance, given a 15 clearances · row a of the head hollow = illegal for this aircraft c DO_NOTHING 3 · ask again? (reselection) again = 1 · again = 0 Bernoulli at (a, c); 0 if no budget left or c = DO_NOTHING to the environment: (a, c, again) log π = log p(a) + log p(c | a) + log p(again | a, c) · entropy: exact, over the whole tree
  1. Which aircraft. The aircraft head scores every slot. The selection mask is applied and one slot is sampled.
  2. Which clearance. The clearance head scores the 15 clearances for the chosen aircraft. That aircraft's row of the clearance mask is applied and one clearance is sampled. Conditioning on the aircraft matters because two aircraft in similar states can have very different legal clearances.
  3. Again? A binary flag is sampled, conditioned on the chosen aircraft and clearance. It is forced to 0 when the again mask is off or the clearance is DO_NOTHING.

The probability of the action is the product of the three stages:

π(a, c, g | o) = π_A(a | o) · π_C(c | a, o) · π_G(g | a, c, o)

In deterministic mode every stage takes its most likely choice instead of sampling. The network that produces the scores is described on Policy network.

docs.title: Reselection
docs.text:
With one clearance per 45 s the agent cannot act on two flights that both need a clearance now. Reselection lets it clear up to two aircraft in one decision interval, and lets the second choice depend on the first.

Reselection. The first pick is queued and the forecast is re-run with it; the second pick is made on the new observation; both clearances are then issued together and the clock advances 45 s.

The steps inside one decision interval are:

  1. From the observation o, the policy picks an aircraft and a clearance (a1, c1) and sets the again flag g1.
  2. If g1 = 0, or c1 is DO_NOTHING, the clearance is executed and the live world advances 45 s. This is an ordinary one-pick step.
  3. If g1 = 1, the clearance is queued. The live clock does not move. The no-operation rollout is recomputed with the queued clearance applied, and the policy receives a new observation o+. In it, aircraft a1 is flagged as cleared in this interval, and all predictions include the effect of c1.
  4. From o+ the policy picks a second pair (a2, c2) with a2 ≠ a1. The again flag is now forced to 0, because the budget of two picks is spent.
  5. Both clearances are executed together and the live world advances 45 s.

The environment never offers a second pick on its own: only the policy asks for one.

simulated time → t t + 45 s the clock does not move between pick 1 and pick 2 pick 1 · observation o flight 4: SLOW_DOWN_MEDIUM again = 1 clearance is queued, not flown reward −0.006 + Φ(o+) − Φ(o) re-predict no-operation rollout with the queued clearance o+: flight 4 now flagged "cleared in this interval" pick 2 · observation o+ flight 6: LENGTHEN_TROMBONE again = 0 (budget spent) flight 4 is masked: it can only be left alone until the clock moves apply and advance both clearances fly together; the simulator advances 45 s reward −0.006 + landing values − 100 · [conflict] + γΦ(o′) − Φ(o+) discounting pick 1 → pick 2: discount 1 (no simulated time passes) pick 2 → next step: discount γ

In the diagram, flights 4 and 6 both need a clearance. The first pick asks for another: its clearance is queued and the forecast is re-run with it, so the second pick already sees flight 4 slowed. The second pick ends the interval. The flight numbers and clearances are illustrative.

This design has two advantages over a joint action. It adds decision bandwidth without building a combinatorial space of clearance pairs: the network still has one aircraft head and one clearance head. And the second decision is conditional on the forecast effect of the first, where two independently sampled clearances could work against each other.

docs.title: The zero-time transition
docs.text:
A queued pick is a transition of the decision process like any other: it has an observation, an action, a reward and a next observation. It differs in that it consumes no simulated time. Two consequences follow.

Its discount is one. In a semi-Markov decision process a transition that lasts a time τ is discounted by γτ. With τ = 0 the factor is exactly 1. Applying the ordinary per-step discount γ would decay the reward artificially each time the policy asked for a second pick, and would skew the critic's value estimates. Equivalently, the two picks can be seen as one temporally extended action, an option: the policy picks (a1, c1), optionally re-selects (a2, c2) after the forecast, and the option ends when the 45 s step has been executed.

Its reward contains no outcome. Nothing moves, so nothing can land and no conflict can occur. The reward of a queued pick is the action cost of its clearance (0.006) plus the change in the shaping potential, Φ(o+) − Φ(o), taken with discount 1. The ordinary transition that follows uses γ Φ(o′) − Φ(o+) with γ = 0.998. Because the shaping uses the same per-transition discount as the learner, it still sums to a difference of potentials over an episode (Objective and reward).

In the code, the environment marks a queued pick with info["zero_time"] = True, and the learner in single-agent/jax_ppo/ppo.py discounts that transition by 1 in the advantage recursion and in the bootstrap at truncation. single-agent/tests/test_multi_pick.py checks that the environment with the again flag always 0 reproduces the one-pick environment exactly, that the masks hold at every pick, and that the shaping telescopes under the per-transition discount.

Reselection is enabled with TADA_MAX_PICKS=2, read at import because it adds the again flag to the action, the two masks to the observation, and one per-aircraft feature ("cleared in the current decision interval", see Observations). Its measured effect during development is in the Research notes.

docs.title: Episodes and temporal windowing
docs.text:
Summary

An episode is one stream of 20 arrivals to one airport. The policy does not see the whole stream: temporal windowing shows it the next 10 flights in the AMAN sequence, in 10 fixed slots. When a flight at the head of the queue lands or is released, the flights behind it move up and the next flight in the queue takes the last slot. Nothing the policy observes, and nothing its critic has to predict, depends on how long the stream is, so the same policy can be run on longer streams. The environment keeps two copies of the traffic: the live world, where clearances are executed, and the predicted world, a do-nothing forecast of it.

Source: single-agent/atc_env/windowed_env.py (class WindowedATCEnv), single-agent/config/windowed_config.py, and the base class in single-agent/atc_env/single_agent_env.py.

docs.title: One episode
docs.text:
An episode starts from a generated scenario: 20 flights bound for one airport, each with an AMAN target landing time. The flights enter the terminal area one after another, the policy issues clearances, and the episode runs until every flight has landed or the episode fails.

The policy acts once every 45 s of simulated time (Config.TIME_BETWEEN_ACTIONS). At each decision it picks one aircraft and one clearance for it, and may ask for a second pick before the clock moves (reselection). The environment then applies the clearances, advances the simulation, and returns a new observation and a reward.

The reinforcement-learning loop. The environment simulates the live world, forecasts it in the predicted world, and builds the observation, the masks and the reward from both.

docs.title: Live world and predicted world
docs.text:
The simulation runs at two levels.

The live world is the traffic as it actually develops. It is integrated in 1 s steps, and clearances are applied to it at the 45 s decision points. Everything that counts as an outcome is read from the live world: landings and their time deviations, conflicts, and aircraft leaving the airspace.

The predicted world is a copy of the live world that is simulated forward with no further clearances. This no-operation rollout shows what will happen if the policy does nothing from now on. It is re-run after every transition, and it provides:

  • the predicted landing time of every flight, and so its predicted time deviation;
  • every predicted proximity event between two aircraft, with its time.

These predictions feed the observation, the shaping terms of the reward, the release rule below and one of the action masks. The predicted world never ends an episode and never decides whether an episode is solved.

The rollout has a receding horizon. It covers 2880 s, or the time until the last flight in the window is due if that is longer, plus a margin of 20 decision steps (900 s) for late flights, and never more than 200 steps. Its length therefore depends on the window and not on the stream. Two details of how landing times are read from it:

  • the simulator reports a landing as mistimed only beyond a tolerance of 10 s, so a flight that the rollout lands within 10 s of its target is predicted exactly on target;
  • a flight that the rollout does not land is placed at the rollout's end, meaning "at least that late".

During reselection the rollout is repeated with the queued clearance applied, so the second pick sees the predicted effect of the first.

docs.title: The window
docs.text: Temporal windowing. The window holds the next 10 flights in AMAN order. When the flight at its head leaves, the others shift up one slot and the next queued flight enters the last slot.

docs.title: Who is in the window
docs.text:
All flights that have not landed and have not been released form a queue, ordered by AMAN target landing time. The window is the first 10 of them.

rule membership the next 10 flights in AMAN order that have neither landed nor been released, whether or not they have entered the terminal area slots slot 1 is the head of the queue; slot order is queue order a flight lands or is released it leaves the window; the flights behind it shift up one slot and the next flight in the queue enters the last slot end of the stream when fewer than 10 flights remain, the trailing slots are empty and masked

The slot index carries no meaning beyond the order: the policy network applies the same encoders to every slot.

docs.title: Pending flights
docs.text:
A flight can hold a slot before it has spawned. Such a pending flight is not yet under control. It is visible to the policy and contributes its schedule and its route, so the policy can plan around it, but it cannot receive a clearance:

  • its row of the clearance mask allows only DO_NOTHING;
  • the aircraft-selection mask offers only flights under control whenever at least one exists.

The policy therefore acts only on flights that are both inside the window and under control.

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
A flight does not have to stay in the window until it touches down. Once its landing is settled it is released: it leaves the window, receives no further clearances, and keeps flying to the runway in the live world. This frees its slot for a flight that still needs attention.

Release works from the head of the queue. After each 45 s step the environment walks down the queue and releases every flight that is locked, stopping at the first one that is not. A flight is locked when all of the following hold:

  • it is under control;
  • the predicted world lands it within the rollout;
  • its predicted landing is within 30 s of its AMAN target (release_dev_s);
  • it is not part of any predicted proximity event.

A released flight is still part of the episode. The flights behind it continue to see it through their landing-gap and conflict features, a conflict that involves it still ends the episode, and its actual landing still counts towards whether the episode is solved. Its landing reward is paid at release from the predicted deviation and corrected at touchdown if the outcome differs (Objective and reward).

At the tail of a stream every airborne flight may already be released. The window then shows those flights again, with only DO_NOTHING legal, so that there is always a slot to pick.

Release is switched on per environment (config key release_locked, with release_dev_s and pay_at_release). Both published policies were trained with it, and the evaluation tools read these keys from each model's run_meta.json so that a policy is always run in the environment it was trained in.

docs.title: What the window hides
docs.text: The price of a fixed window is explicit partial observability: a flight that is under control but more than ten places behind the head of the queue is not represented. The environment counts the decision steps on which this happens and reports the fraction in the episode metrics as window_overflow_frac.

docs.title: Stream-stationary observables
docs.text:
The design rule of the windowed environment is that nothing the policy observes, and nothing its critic has to predict, may depend on how many flights the stream has. A 20-flight scenario is treated as a finite excerpt of an endless arrival stream. Five things follow from the rule:

  • The forecast covers the window, not the scenario (the receding horizon above).
  • Time features are relative. Each flight carries its scheduled time to its target, and the global time feature is the time until the last flight in the window is due. Absolute scenario time does not appear.
  • Counts and maxima are taken over the window. The global count is the number of window flights under control, not the number of occupied slots, which would only fall as the stream ran out. The global conflict feature is the maximum over the flights in the window.
  • The reward is paid per flight, once, and the penalty for a conflict is a constant. Neither scales with the number of flights left.
  • The end of the stream is not a terminal state (next section).

The observation features themselves are described on Observations.

docs.title: Termination and truncation
docs.text:
event in the live world signal end_reason a conflict: two aircraft within 3 NM and 500 ft terminated separation an aircraft leaves the airspace terminated airspace_exit every flight has landed truncated success if every flight is within 60 s of its target, otherwise delayed the step limit is reached truncated timeout

A conflict or an airspace exit is a true termination. The episode stops at once and the reward carries a fixed penalty. Only realised events count: a predicted conflict never terminates an episode (Separation rules).

The stream running dry is reported as a truncation, not a termination. In a continuing stream more flights would follow, and the critic sees only the window, not how many flights remain. PPO therefore bootstraps from the critic's value at that point instead of treating it as an absorbing end. An episode with end_reason = "success" is a solved episode.

The step limit is sized per scenario: the number of 45 s steps to the last target landing time, plus 6, and at least 48. Training caps it at 200 steps per 20-flight segment. The evaluation scripts lift the cap, so every stream runs to its own horizon.

A zero-time reselection pick cannot end an episode, because nothing moves.

docs.title: The scenario for each procedure
docs.text:
One environment class serves both procedures. The procedure is a property of the scenario, chosen by the use case:

TMB PMS airport, procedure Milan Malpensa, trombone Milan Bergamo, point merge use case 1 (MissionDifficulty.VALIDATION_USE_CASE_1, the default) 2 (MissionDifficulty.VALIDATION_USE_CASE_2) generator settings single-agent/config/simulation_config_mxp/ single-agent/config/simulation_config_bgy/ clearance set (TADA_ACTION_SET) v2 v2pms routes at the start of an episode cut to the short AMAN route; trombone levels stored for lengthen the whole sequencing leg kept; shortened by direct to merge point

The use case is selected in three places:

  • the environment config key use_case (1 or 2), recorded in the model's run_meta.json;
  • python main_jax.py --use-case 1|2 when training;
  • python -m evaluation.run_search --procedure tmb|pms, or --use-case on analysis.score_windowed, when evaluating.

With TADA_GENERATOR=procedure (the default) the scenario generator reads the settings directory that belongs to the use case, and the first scenario that a seed draws is used: there is no rejection filter. The clearance set has to match the procedure: v2pms refuses a route without a merge point, and loading a model under a clearance set other than the one in its run_meta.json stops with an error. The clearance sets are described on Actions and reselection.

docs.title: Longer and stitched streams
docs.text:
Because of the design rule above, stream length is only a setting of the environment (scenario_aircraft_count). Training uses this for its curriculum, which starts on 10-flight streams and then moves to 20 (Train a policy). The published policies were evaluated on single 20-flight streams. The public code also supports two kinds of longer stream.

A longer generated stream. --flights 40 on analysis.score_windowed generates 40 flights in one sequence.

A stitched stream. A stream is built from several independently generated 20-flight segments (Simulator._stitched_scenario in single-agent/simulator/simulator.py):

  • the first target landing of each further segment comes a random cooling gap after the last target landing of the previous one, drawn uniformly from 120 to 900 s by default;
  • the spawn times and targets of a segment shift together, so its internal spacing is untouched;
  • callsigns and stored trombone sections are renumbered to continue the queue.

For a fixed seed the segments and the gaps are deterministic. With stitching, the step limit grows with the number of segments, and the cost of a clearance is divided by it, so that the priority order of the objectives is kept on the longer stream.

option training python main_jax.py --stitch-segments 2 --stitch-gap 120 900 scoring python -m analysis.score_windowed --segments 2 --gap 120 900 rendering python render_policy.py --env windowed --segments 2

analysis/long_stream_seeds.py screens seeds for stitched streams that are feasible: by default, streams in which no flight is predicted to land more than 650 s early when no clearance is given. The experiments with long streams during development are in the Research notes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Defaults from single-agent/config/windowed_config.py (WindowedConfig) and single-agent/config/config.py (Config):
